questions.question:
Consider the two lists List I and List II given below:
[latex] \begin{array}{|c l|c l|} \hline \textbf{List I} & & \textbf{List II} & \\ \hline \text{(i)} & \text{Context free languages} & \text{(a)} & \text{Closed under union} \\ \hline \text{(ii)} & \text{Recursive languages} & \text{(b)} & \text{Not closed under complementation} \\ \hline \text{(iii)} & \text{Regular languages} & \text{(c)} & \text{Closed under intersection} \\ \hline \end{array}[/latex]
For matching of items in List I with those in List II, which of the following option(s) is/are CORRECT?

options.C: (i) - (b), (ii) - (c), and (iii) - (a)

questions.explanation:
Recall the closure properties: Context-free languages are closed under union, but famously not closed under complementation (matching (i)-(b)) and also not closed under intersection in general. Recursive languages and regular languages are each closed under both union and intersection (both (a) and (c) hold true for each of them) — so either valid assignment of (a)/(c) across (ii) and (iii) gives a fully correct matching, as long as (i) is paired with (b) (the one property that specifically distinguishes CFLs from the other two classes).

This is exactly why two different complete matchings both check out as correct: (i)-(b), (ii)-(a), (iii)-(c) and (i)-(b), (ii)-(c), (iii)-(a) — since recursive and regular languages don't care which of (a)/(c) is assigned to which, both being true of both.

Answer: (i)-(b),(ii)-(a),(iii)-(c) AND (i)-(b),(ii)-(c),(iii)-(a)

questions.question: Which of the following statements is/are CORRECT?

options.A: The intersection of two regular languages is regular.
options.B: The intersection of two context-free languages is context-free.
options.C: The intersection of two recursive languages is recursive.
options.D: The intersection of two recursively enumerable languages is recursively enumerable.

questions.explanation:
Checking each statement:
- Regular languages are closed under intersection [latex]\text{---}[/latex] TRUE.
- CFLs are not closed under intersection: [latex]a^nb^nc^m\cap a^mb^nc^n=a^nb^nc^n[/latex] [latex]\text{---}[/latex] FALSE.
- Recursive: run both deciders, accept if both accept [latex]\text{---}[/latex] TRUE.
- RE: run both recognizers, accept when both accept [latex]\text{---}[/latex] TRUE.

Answer: Options 1, 3 and 4

questions.question: A regular language [latex]L[/latex] is accepted by a non-deterministic finite automaton (NFA) with [latex]n[/latex] states. Which of the following statement(s) is/are FALSE?

options.A: [latex]L[/latex] may have an accepting NFA with < [latex]n[/latex] states.
options.B: [latex]L[/latex] may have an accepting DFA with < [latex]n[/latex] states.
options.C: There exists a DFA with [latex]\leq 2^n[/latex] states that accepts [latex]L[/latex].
options.D: Every DFA that accepts [latex]L[/latex] has [latex]> 2^n[/latex] states.

questions.explanation:
For a regular language [latex]L[/latex] accepted by some [latex]n[/latex]-state NFA, recall two standard facts: (1) subset construction always produces an equivalent DFA with at most [latex]2^n[/latex] states, and (2) NFA/DFA state counts for a given language are not unique — smaller equivalent automata can certainly exist.

- "[latex]L[/latex] may have an accepting NFA with [latex]< n[/latex] states": could well be true (this [latex]n[/latex]-state NFA might not be minimal), so calling it FALSE is incorrect — it's a true possibility, not a false statement.
- "[latex]L[/latex] may have an accepting DFA with [latex]< n[/latex] states": also entirely possible depending on the language, so this is also true (not false).
- "There exists a DFA with [latex]\le 2^n[/latex] states accepting [latex]L[/latex]": guaranteed true by subset construction — so this is also true, not false.
- "Every DFA that accepts L has [latex]> 2^n[/latex] states": this directly contradicts the subset-construction guarantee (a DFA with at most [latex]2^n[/latex] states always exists) — so this statement is definitely FALSE.

Answer: "Every DFA that accepts L has more than [latex]2^n[/latex] states" is the FALSE statement.

questions.question: Let [latex]L_1, L_2 [/latex] be two regular languages and [latex]L_3 [/latex] a language which is not regular. Which of the following statements is/are always TRUE?

options.C: [latex]\overline{L_3} [/latex] is not regular

questions.explanation:
Checking each statement:
- [latex]L_1\cap\overline{L_2}=\phi[/latex] only means [latex]L_1\subseteq L_2[/latex]. Equality also needs [latex]L_2\subseteq L_1[/latex] [latex]\text{---}[/latex] FALSE.
- [latex]L_1\cup L_3[/latex] can be regular: take [latex]L_1=\Sigma^*[/latex], then [latex]L_1\cup L_3=\Sigma^*[/latex] [latex]\text{---}[/latex] FALSE (not always).
- If [latex]\overline{L_3}[/latex] were regular, then its complement [latex]L_3[/latex] would be regular (closure under complement). So [latex]\overline{L_3}[/latex] is not regular [latex]\text{---}[/latex] TRUE.
- Regular languages are closed under complement and union, so [latex]\overline{L_1}\cup\overline{L_2}[/latex] is regular [latex]\text{---}[/latex] TRUE.

Answer: [latex]\overline{L_3}[/latex] is not regular; [latex]\overline{L_1}\cup\overline{L_2}[/latex] is regular

questions.question:
Consider the language [latex]L=\{a^n|n\geq 0\}\cup \{a^nb^n|n\geq 0\}[/latex] and the following statements.

I. L is deterministic context-free.
II. L is context-free but not deterministic context-free.
III. L is not LL(k) for any k.

Which of the above statements is/are TRUE?

options.C: I and III only

questions.explanation:
Checking each statement:
- A DPDA can push a's and, on reading b's, pop them; it accepts if it is still on a's or the counts match. So L is deterministic CFL [latex]\text{---}[/latex] I TRUE, II FALSE.
- An LL(k) parser must decide at the start whether the string is [latex]a^n[/latex] or [latex]a^nb^n[/latex], but with long runs of a's, k symbols of lookahead are not enough [latex]\text{---}[/latex] III TRUE.

Answer: I and III only

questions.question:
Consider the following context-free grammar over the alphabet [latex]\sum[/latex] = {a,b,c} with S as the start symbol.

S[latex]\rightarrow[/latex]abScT|abcT
T[latex]\rightarrow[/latex]bT|b

Which one of the following represents the language generated by the above grammar ?

options.C: [latex](ab)^{n}(cb^{m})^{n}|n,m\geq 1[/latex]

questions.explanation:
Each use of [latex]S\rightarrow abScT[/latex] adds an "ab" on the left and a "cT" on the right; the last step [latex]S\rightarrow abcT[/latex] adds one more pair. T gives [latex]b^m[/latex] with m [latex]\ge[/latex] 1, chosen separately each time.

So: [latex](ab)^n\,cb^{m_1}cb^{m_2}\ldots cb^{m_n}[/latex] with all [latex]m_i\ge1[/latex].

Answer: Option 2

[latex] L2=\{0^{p}1^{q}|p,q\in N and p=q\} [/latex] and
[latex]L3=\{0^{p}1^{q}0^{r}|p,q,r\in N \; and \; p=q=r\}[/latex]

options.A: Push Down Automata (PDA) can be used to recognize L1 and L2
options.C: All the three languages are context free

questions.question:
Consider the 5 -state DFA [latex] M [/latex] accepting the language [latex] L(M) \subset(0+1)^* [/latex] shown below. For any string [latex] w \in(0+1)^* [/latex] let [latex] n_0(w) [/latex] be the number of [latex] 0^{\prime} s [/latex] in [latex] w [/latex] and [latex] n_1(w) [/latex] be the number of 1 's in [latex] w [/latex].

Which of the following statements is/are FALSE?

options.A: States 2 and 4 are distinguishable in [latex] M [/latex]
options.B: States 3 and 4 are distinguishable in [latex] M [/latex]
options.C: States 2 and 5 are distinguishable in [latex] M [/latex]
options.D: Any string [latex] w [/latex] with [latex] n_0(w)=n_1(w) [/latex] is in [latex] L(M) [/latex]

questions.explanation:
Reading 0 moves 1[latex]\rightarrow[/latex]2[latex]\rightarrow[/latex]3[latex]\rightarrow[/latex]1, reading 1 moves 1[latex]\rightarrow[/latex]4[latex]\rightarrow[/latex]5[latex]\rightarrow[/latex]1, and the reverse arrows undo a step. So the DFA tracks [latex](n_0-n_1)\bmod 3[/latex]:
state 1 = 0, states 2 and 5 = 1, states 3 and 4 = 2.

[latex]L(M)=\{w: n_0(w)\equiv n_1(w)\pmod 3\}[/latex], and states with the same value are equivalent.

- 2 and 4 (values 1 and 2): distinguishable (input "1": 2[latex]\rightarrow[/latex]1 accept, 4[latex]\rightarrow[/latex]5 reject) [latex]\text{---}[/latex] TRUE.
- 3 and 4: both value 2 [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] equivalent [latex]\text{---}[/latex] statement FALSE.
- 2 and 5: both value 1 [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] equivalent [latex]\text{---}[/latex] statement FALSE.
- [latex]n_0=n_1[/latex] [latex]\Rightarrow[/latex] difference 0 [latex]\Rightarrow[/latex] accepted [latex]\text{---}[/latex] TRUE.

Answer: "States 3 and 4 are distinguishable" and "States 2 and 5 are distinguishable"

questions.question:
Consider the following context-free grammar [latex]G[/latex].

[latex] \begin{array}{l} S \rightarrow a b a A B A b b a \\ A \rightarrow a a B B A b \mid b B a b a a \\ B \rightarrow a B b \mid a b \end{array} [/latex]

In the above grammar, [latex]S[/latex] is the start symbol, [latex]a[/latex] and [latex]b[/latex] are terminal symbols, and [latex]A[/latex] and [latex]B[/latex] are non-terminal symbols.

Let [latex]L(G)[/latex] be the language generated by the grammar [latex]G[/latex]. For a string [latex]s \in L(G)[/latex], let [latex]n_{1}(s)[/latex] be the number of [latex]a[/latex] 's in [latex]s[/latex] and [latex]n_{2}(s)[/latex] be the number of [latex]b[/latex] 's in [latex]s[/latex].

Which of the following statements is/are true?

options.A: There is a string [latex]s \in L(G)[/latex] such that [latex]n_{1}(s) < n_{2}(s)[/latex]
options.B: For every string [latex]s \in L(G), n_{1}(s) \geq n_{2}(s)[/latex]
options.C: There is a string [latex]s \in L(G)[/latex] such that [latex]n_{1}(s)>2 n_{2}(s)[/latex]
options.D: For every string [latex]s \in L(G), n_{1}(s) \leq 2 n_{2}(s)[/latex]

questions.explanation:
[latex]B\rightarrow aBb\mid ab[/latex] always generates strings of the form [latex]a^kb^k[/latex] ([latex]k\ge1[/latex]) — equal numbers of [latex]a[/latex]'s and [latex]b[/latex]'s, i.e. [latex]n_1=n_2[/latex] within any string derived from [latex]B[/latex].

[latex]A\rightarrow aaBBAb\mid bBabaa[/latex]: substituting the fact that each [latex]B[/latex]-string contributes equal [latex]a[/latex]'s and [latex]b[/latex]'s, and tracking the extra fixed terminals in each production, one can verify by induction that every string derivable from [latex]A[/latex] satisfies [latex]n_1(s)\ge n_2(s)[/latex] (the fixed terminal parts always contribute at least as many, often more, [latex]a[/latex]'s as [latex]b[/latex]'s on top of the balanced [latex]B[/latex]-parts), and also that [latex]n_1(s)\le 2\,n_2(s)[/latex] always (the excess of [latex]a[/latex]'s over [latex]b[/latex]'s is bounded relative to the total [latex]b[/latex] count, because of the specific fixed ratio of terminals baked into each production).

[latex]S\rightarrow abaABAbba[/latex] adds a further fixed collection of terminals ([latex]4[/latex] [latex]a[/latex]'s and [latex]4[/latex] [latex]b[/latex]'s from the frame, plus two copies of an [latex]A[/latex]-string), and this fixed frame preserves the same two invariants that hold for [latex]A[/latex]: every generated string has [latex]n_1(s)\ge n_2(s)[/latex] and [latex]n_1(s)\le2\,n_2(s)[/latex], with no derivable string ever violating either bound.

Answer: For every string s ∈ L(G), [latex]n_1(s)\ge n_2(s)[/latex]; and for every string s ∈ L(G), [latex]n_1(s)\le2n_2(s)[/latex].

questions.question:
Let [latex]\Sigma = \{a, b, c\} [/latex]. For [latex]x \in \Sigma^* [/latex], and [latex]\alpha \in \Sigma [/latex], let [latex]\# _\alpha (x) [/latex] denote the number of occurrences of [latex]\alpha [/latex] in [latex]x [/latex].

Which one or more of the following option(s) define(s) regular language(s)?

options.B: [latex]\{ a, b \}^* \cap \{ a^m b^n c^{m-n} \mid m \geq n \geq 0 \} [/latex]
options.C: [latex]\{ w \mid w \in \{ a, b \}^*, \#_a(w) \equiv 2 \ (\text{mod}\ 7), \#_b(w) \equiv 3 \ (\text{mod}\ 9) \} [/latex]

questions.explanation:
[latex]\{a^mb^n\mid m,n\ge0\}[/latex]: simply any number of [latex]a[/latex]'s followed by any number of [latex]b[/latex]'s, with no relationship required between the two counts — matched exactly by the regular expression [latex]a^*b^*[/latex]. Regular.

[latex]\{a,b\}^*\cap\{a^mb^nc^{m-n}\mid m\ge n\ge0\}[/latex]: intersecting with [latex]\{a,b\}^*[/latex] (strings with no [latex]c[/latex]'s at all) forces [latex]c^{m-n}[/latex] to be the empty string, i.e. [latex]m=n[/latex] exactly. This leaves exactly [latex]\{a^nb^n\mid n\ge0\}[/latex] — the classic non-regular language (requires unbounded exact-count matching). Not regular.

[latex]\{w\mid\#_a(w)\equiv2\pmod7,\ \#_b(w)\equiv3\pmod9\}[/latex]: despite unbounded counts of [latex]a[/latex]'s and [latex]b[/latex]'s, only their values modulo a fixed number matter, which needs only [latex]7\times9=63[/latex] distinct states to track (a finite automaton cycling through remainders). Regular.

[latex]\{w\mid\#_a(w)\equiv2\pmod7,\ \#_a(w)=\#_b(w)\}[/latex]: the modular part alone would be fine, but the additional requirement of exact equality between [latex]\#_a(w)[/latex] and [latex]\#_b(w)[/latex] (unbounded, not just modular) needs unbounded memory. Not regular.

Answer: {a^m b^n} and the mod-7/mod-9 language are both regular.

questions.question:
Consider the pushdown automaton (PDA) [latex]P[/latex] below, which runs on the input alphabet [latex]\{a,b\}[/latex], has stack alphabet [latex] \{ \perp ,A\}[/latex], and has three states [latex] \{s,p,q\}[/latex], with [latex]s[/latex] being the start state. A transition from state [latex]u[/latex] to state [latex]v[/latex] , labelled [latex]c/X/\gamma [/latex] , where [latex]c[/latex] is an input symbol or , [latex]X[/latex] is a stack symbol, and [latex]\gamma [/latex] is a string of stack symbols, represents the fact that in state [latex]u[/latex], the PDA can read [latex]c[/latex] from the input, with [latex]X[/latex] on the top of its stack, pop [latex]X[/latex] from the stack, push in the string [latex]\gamma [/latex] on the stack, and go to state [latex]v[/latex]. In the initial configuration, the stack has only the symbol [latex]\perp [/latex] in it. The PDA accepts by empty stack.

Which one of the following options correctly describes the language accepted by [latex]P[/latex]?

options.C: [latex] \{ a^mb^n |0\leq m\text{ and } 0 \lt n \}[/latex]

questions.explanation:
Read the PDA transitions:
- In s, every a pushes an A (so m a's give m A's).
- The first b moves to p and pops an A; each further b pops another A.
- To empty the stack we must go to q, and both moves into q need an A on top. In q, the remaining A's and [latex]\perp[/latex] are popped.

So at least one A must be left after reading the b's: [latex]n \lt m[/latex], and [latex]m\ge1[/latex] (with no a's there is no A to move to q).

Answer: [latex]\{a^mb^n\mid 1\le m,\ n \lt m\}[/latex]

- 0*(10*1)*0* cannot make "101".
- Option 4 needs at least two 1s, so it misses "0".

Answer: 0*(10*10*)*

questions.question:
Consider the following languages.
L1 = {[latex]\lt[/latex]M[latex]\gt[/latex] |M takes at least 2016 steps on some input},
L2 = {[latex]\lt[/latex]M[latex]\gt[/latex]| M takes at least 2016 steps on all inputs} and
L3 = {[latex]\lt[/latex]M|M accepts [latex]\varepsilon[/latex]},
where for each Turing machine M, [latex]\lt[/latex]M[latex]\gt[/latex] denotes a specific encoding of M. Which one of the following is TRUE?

options.A: L1 is recursive and L2,L3 are notrecursive
options.B: L2 is recursiveand L1,L3 are notrecursive
options.C: L1,L2 are recursiveand L3 is notrecursive

questions.explanation:
In 2016 steps a TM reads at most the first 2016 input symbols, so only inputs of length up to 2016 matter. Simulating M on all of them for 2016 steps decides both L1 and L2 [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] recursive.

L3 (M accepts [latex]\varepsilon[/latex]) is a non-trivial property of L(M) [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] undecidable (Rice).

Answer: L1, L2 are recursive and L3 is not recursive

questions.question: Let X be a recursive language and Y be a recursively enumerable but not recursive language. Let W and Z be two languages such that [latex]\bar{Y}[/latex]  reduces to W, and Z reduces to [latex]\bar{X}[/latex] (reduction means the standard many-one-reduction). Which one of the following statements is TRUE?

options.A: W can be recursively enumerable and Z is recursive.
options.B: W can be recursive and Z is recursively enumerable
options.C: W is not recursively enumerable and Z is recursive
options.D: W is not recursively enumerable and Z is not recursive.

questions.explanation:
Checking each statement:
- Y is RE but not recursive, so [latex]\bar Y[/latex] is not RE. Since [latex]\bar Y[/latex] reduces to W, W cannot be RE (otherwise [latex]\bar Y[/latex] would be).
- X is recursive, so [latex]\bar X[/latex] is recursive. Z reduces to [latex]\bar X[/latex], so Z is recursive.

Answer: W is not recursively enumerable and Z is recursive
